comments.body:
## Measured: the memory signal is published ~27% of the time — AC4 quantified

Taken 2026-09-06 ~00:30Z, roughly 90 minutes AFTER the stop/start recovery, on a healthy idle host:

```
mem_available_percent    5/18 five-minute buckets = 27% coverage
mcp_healthy (head of script) 12/18                = 66% coverage
```

Same window, same probe run. The difference is position in `observability.sh`: `mcp_healthy`
publishes near line 131, the memory reading later, and the probe is truncated before reaching the
tail (`ignitable-fuchsia-kawala`). This is the same monotone presence-vs-position gradient measured
independently earlier: ~93% at lines 112-213 falling to ~43% at 1463/1511.

**Consequence for this ticket:** the run-up telemetry AC4 asks for does not merely have gaps, it is
absent about three times out of four. On the outage day the metric showed 11-13% available for
hours and then NOTHING for ~5 hours immediately before the wedge. At 27% coverage we would still
miss most of a repeat.

## This reprioritises change 2684

Change 2684 (`Compose the observability probe's time budget`, currently `Verified +1` awaiting
review) has been treated as an alarm-noise fix. It is not — it is the PREREQUISITE for this
ticket's AC2 ("the next occurrence is diagnosable from data alone"). Without it, adding a memory
alarm produces an alarm on a signal that is absent three quarters of the time, which is a
missing-data pager rather than a memory detector.

Recommended sequencing for whoever works this: land 2684 first, confirm coverage rises, THEN add
the `mem_available_percent` threshold alarm. Adding the alarm first inverts the value — it will
fire on absence rather than on memory.

## Also observed, recorded as a value not a finding

The last two readings in the window moved 66% -> 34%. Both are healthy and two points are not a
trend; recorded only because 34% is the first sub-40% reading since recovery and the baseline for
"normal after restart" is not yet established.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## Why the cause was unprovable is now itself proven — and a second outage gave us the mechanism

Two things landed tonight that materially advance this ticket without closing it.

### 1. The missing memory data has a root cause, and it is not "the host died"

This ticket could not prove a memory hypothesis because the memory series was absent across the
incident window. That absence is now explained, and it is a **defect in the probe, not evidence
about the host**:

`observability.sh` resolves its four cap scripts as siblings of its own installed path
(`/usr/local/bin/`), but two of those scripts' `--install` writes a **`rebar-`-prefixed** name,
because that path is the `ExecStart` of the reaper units they render. So the probe called
`vartmp-cap.sh` / `container-cap.sh`, got `rc=127 No such file or directory`, and their
`--print-env` returned nothing — leaving the budget variables unset and the publish guards false.
The probe's own log states it: `var_tmp /var/tmp budget=unsetB cleanup_active=0`.

Confirmed by a natural experiment, 4 for 4: the two cap scripts that DO sit in `/usr/local/bin`
(from a manual operator copy) publish their percentages; the two absent ones publish nothing.
Fix is Gerrit **2722**.

Separately, `mem_available_percent` was measured publishing **zero datapoints for five consecutive
hours** (12:00-16:00 PDT) while `mcp_healthy` published 7-12/hour in the same probe runs — a
head-vs-tail truncation gradient. So during exactly the window this ticket needed data, the
publisher was silently dropping its tail. **The evidence was never collected; it was not lost.**

### 2. A second outage tonight, with a PROVEN memory mechanism

At 02:09-02:44 UTC the host wedged again, and this time the cause is known and attributable: an
agent ran `lsof +D /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch`, which recursed 226 snapshot directories.
Available memory fell **43% -> 33% -> 23% -> 21% -> 4%**, SSM stopped pinging at 19:09:18 PDT, all
`rebar/host` metrics stopped at 19:08, and it did not self-recover in ~30 minutes. Recovery was an
EC2 `reboot-instances` (SSM back in 4m20s), with EBS snapshots taken first
(`snap-01e10c794b7abcf0e`, `snap-0bae90f11fb67532b`). Nothing was lost.

This does **not** prove the original outage had the same cause. What it does establish, on this
exact host, is that **memory exhaustion alone is sufficient to produce the observed signature** —
TLS, then SSM, then TCP failing in that order, with EC2 status checks reading `ok` throughout
because the hypervisor is fine. That was previously a hypothesis; it is now a demonstrated
mechanism with a measured memory trajectory. Worth noting the runbook had warned about this class:
`gate-scratch-mount.md` §1 records that a plain `du -sh` over that directory never finished in 25
minutes, and says the runbook "therefore never depends on `du`".

### 3. Two contributing conditions are now removed

- **Gate scratch is off the root filesystem.** The volume is mounted (xfs, by UUID, `nofail`), and
  root fell **70% -> 29%** (~23 GiB reclaimed). A review burst can no longer fill the OS disk.
- **`/var/tmp` reclaimed 3664 MiB -> 1 MiB** (rehearsal debris, every file >7 days old).

Available memory now reads **58%** at load 0.74, against 11-13% under load earlier.

### What this ticket still needs

The original outage's cause remains **unproven**, and I am not closing it on the above. What has
changed is that the instrument is being repaired: once 2722 lands and the probe publishes its full
metric set, a recurrence would leave the evidence this one did not. The honest status is "cause
still unproven; the reason it was unprovable is fixed, and one sufficient mechanism is now
demonstrated on this host." If the memory series is intact at the next incident and shows the same
trajectory, that closes it. If an incident occurs WITH intact memory data and memory looks healthy,
that refutes the memory hypothesis outright — which is the falsifiable test this ticket has lacked.

comments.body:
OBSERVATION
Partial RCA verified. The ticket already had the essential evidence: original 2026-09-05 outage remained unprovable because host-side memory telemetry was absent in the run-up, while hypervisor metrics survived. I re-queried CloudWatch read-only (us-east-1, i-00880b2c7f13527c5). During the original outage window, NetworkIn collapsed to tiny 5-minute sums at 16:30-16:45 PDT while CPU fell and StatusCheckFailed stayed 0; mem_available_percent had no datapoints until 17:00 PDT, after recovery. A later 18:30-20:10 PDT recurrence did capture mem_available_percent dropping 43 -> 33 -> 23 -> 21 -> 4 before host metrics went dark, then returning after reboot.

HYPOTHESIS
Original cause remains unproven, but the proven RCA for unprovability is the observability path: infra/scripts/observability.sh publishes mem_available_percent late in the probe, and the ticket's prior comments identify probe truncation / missing cap-script budget setup as why the tail metric was not reliably emitted. The demonstrated sufficient outage mechanism is host memory exhaustion: when available memory reached 4%, the same service-degradation shape occurred while EC2 status checks remained green.

CONFIRMATION
CloudWatch experiments were read-only and bounded by finite get-metric-statistics calls. Evidence that would disprove the telemetry-gap RCA would be a complete pre-23:28 memory series for the original incident; the metric was absent in the queried outage run-up. Evidence that would disprove memory as a sufficient mechanism would be the later recurrence lacking a memory collapse; instead it showed the 43% -> 4% descent before recovery.

SUGGESTED FIX DIRECTION
Treat this as PARTIAL for the original outage: do not assert memory caused it. First make host memory publishing reliable and early enough to capture the run-up; then alarm on sustained low memory and optionally on the hypervisor-visible NetworkIn-collapse signature. Design needed for telemetry/alarm policy, not a simple code fix.

compiled_state.description:
## Summary

The Gerrit host (`i-00880b2c7f13527c5`, `t4g.large`) became totally unresponsive for ~28 minutes on
2026-09-05. A soft reboot did NOT clear it; a stop/start recovered it in under 3 minutes. **The
cause is NOT established**, and the reason it is not established is a specific, fixable telemetry
gap.

## Timeline (UTC)

```
~22:0x   intermittent HTTP 504 on git fetch (nginx Gerrit location on the 60s default
         proxy_read_timeout while upload-pack legitimately runs to ~144s — antihuman-beefwitted-zebra)
 23:13   NetworkIn SPIKE: 9.6 MB avg vs ~1.0 MB baseline (10x)
 23:19   CI checkout for change 2689 fails with the 504 signature
 23:26   SSM agent last ping
 23:28   NetworkIn COLLAPSES to 1,829 bytes / 5-min period and stays there
 ~23:3x  TLS handshakes stop completing; TCP connect still succeeds (0.085s)
 ~23:4x  TCP connect itself times out
 23:47   soft reboot issued — INEFFECTIVE (SSM still Undeliverable, TLS still dead)
 23:51   stop/start issued
 23:54   RECOVERED: http=200, TLS 0.18s, git ls-remote exit 0, SSM PingStatus Online
```

Failure order was TLS -> SSM -> TCP: services degraded before the kernel stopped accepting.

## RULED OUT, with data

- **EBS burst exhaustion.** `EBSIOBalance%` fell only to **61.6%** and `EBSByteBalance%` to
  **65.2%**; neither approached zero. Recovered to 99% after restart.
- **CPU saturation.** `CPUUtilization` FELL through the incident: 70 -> 68 -> 60 -> 47 -> 18 -> 24
  -> 28%. A CPU pin looks nothing like this. (`CPUCreditBalance` was 0.00 and
  `CPUSurplusCreditBalance` ~361, so the instance was throttled to its 30% baseline — utilisation
  reading ~28% is consistent with work QUEUING behind a cap, not with CPU being the binding cause.)
- **Hypervisor-visible failure.** `StatusCheckFailed` was **0.00** for the entire window; EC2
  reported `running / system ok / instance ok` while the host was completely unreachable.
- **Disk pressure** — the previously-established failure mode (bug 3276). Root disk was 71-76%
  against an 85% threshold before the incident. Not implicated.

## The signature, and the leading unmeasured candidate

`NetworkIn` collapsing to ~2 KB per period at 23:28 is the clearest marker — the host stopped
transacting. The 10x spike at 23:13, fifteen minutes earlier, is a LEAD and nothing more; it was
not correlated to a specific workload.

**Memory is the one major resource AWS does not publish at the hypervisor level.** `rebar-mcp` was
independently measured at **4.45 GB RSS (55.6% of 7.8 GiB)** earlier the same evening, squeezing
page cache to ~600 MB on a git server. Memory exhaustion (OOM, or swap thrash, which presents as
low CPU with everything blocked) fits every observation — falling CPU, collapsing network, TLS
failing before TCP, SSM agent dying, and a soft reboot failing where a power cycle worked. **It is
NOT established.** It is the leading candidate precisely because it is the thing we did not measure.

## The telemetry gap — this is the actionable part

We had EC2 hypervisor metrics only. Everything host-side went dark with the host:

1. **No memory metric survives to CloudWatch.** The rebar probe publishes `mem_used_percent`, but
   `ignitable-fuchsia-kawala` shows the probe is SIGTERM-ed on its 4-minute timeout with ~42 s of
   CPU consumed, and its tail metrics degraded to roughly 1 datapoint in 3 hours. So the one
   memory signal we have is the least reliable thing we publish.
2. **The SSM agent died at 23:26**, removing the only interactive channel. Diagnosis after that
   point was impossible.
3. The reframing that matters: **we do not need telemetry that survives the outage — we need
   telemetry that captures the RUN-UP.** A memory series with 5-minute resolution for the twenty
   minutes before 23:28 would very likely settle this. That series should exist and does not,
   because the publisher truncates.

Change **2684** (`ignitable-fuchsia-kawala`) has since landed and closed after a superseded patchset-1 `Verified +1`, a real patchset-2 `Verified -1`, and a patchset-3 fix. Later monitoring work also added `infra/terraform/monitoring_membound.tf`, including host memory and missing-memory-signal alarms. This ticket therefore does not need to invent a second publisher; the remaining in-scope work is to (1) verify the already-merged memory publisher/alarm path with current tests and (2) update the shell-free recovery runbook so the next total outage can be diagnosed from off-box data rather than SSM access.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1 A host memory series reaches CloudWatch reliably enough to show a 20-minute run-up,
      surviving the probe's truncation behaviour. State whether this rides on 2684's fix or needs
      an independent publisher, and justify.
- [ ] AC2 The next occurrence is diagnosable from data alone, without SSM access. Name the specific
      metrics that would discriminate memory exhaustion from the alternatives.
- [ ] AC3 An alarm fires on the RUN-UP (e.g. sustained memory above a threshold), not only on the
      aftermath. An alarm that fires when the host is already gone has no operational value.
- [ ] AC4 The NetworkIn collapse signature is evaluated as a detector: it is hypervisor-published,
      so it survives host death. Decide whether it is worth alarming on and record the reasoning.
- [ ] AC5 The 23:13 NetworkIn spike is attributed to a workload, or explicitly recorded as
      unattributed.

## Related

`ignitable-fuchsia-kawala` (probe truncation, change 2684), `relevant-dissident-salamander`, `antihuman-beefwitted-zebra`, `witted-invisible-roan`, and `lousy-unsuited-gnu`.

## Implementation plan

- Add a memory-exhaustion / telemetry-survival section to `infra/runbooks/gerrit-host-wedged-ssm-lost.md`, extending the existing wedged-host runbook rather than creating a duplicate runbook. The new section will name the run-up metrics (`mem_available_percent`, `mem_used_percent`, `container_memory_rss_bytes`, `mem_probe_ok`, `container_stats_ok`), the already-merged alarms (`rebar-host-memory-low`, `rebar-mem-signal-absent-while-probe-alive`, `rebar-memory-probe-not-ok`), the alternatives to rule out (`CPUUtilization`, `StatusCheckFailed`, EBS burst/root-disk metrics), the NetworkIn-collapse decision, and the still-unattributed 23:13 NetworkIn spike.
- Create `tests/unit/test_gerrit_wedged_runbook_memory.py` to pin that runbook content so future edits cannot erase the memory/NetworkIn diagnostic contract.
- Do not change Terraform unless inspection shows `monitoring_membound.tf` no longer declares the current memory alarms; the current implementation already has the off-box alarm path.

## Testing / Verification

- Run `pytest tests/scripts/test_observability_memory_9ea3.py tests/unit/test_alarm_actions_terraform.py tests/unit/test_alarm_window_tuning.py -q` to verify the existing publisher/alarm path: memory datapoints are emitted by `observability.sh`, memory probe/container-stats health is surfaced, and the host memory alarms remain wired to actions/windows.
- Run `pytest tests/unit/test_gerrit_wedged_runbook_memory.py -q` after creating it to prove the identified shell-free runbook file names the memory telemetry survival path, discriminating metrics, NetworkIn-collapse decision, and unattributed 23:13 spike.
- Run `terraform -chdir=infra/terraform validate` only if Terraform alarm declarations change; otherwise record that no Terraform diff was needed because the already-merged memory alarms satisfy AC3.
- Run `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM=/dev/null make verify PYTEST_WORKERS=2` before push, dropping to `PYTEST_WORKERS=1` only for a low-memory environmental death.

Pin the runbook evidence so future edits do not erase the memory/NetworkIn diagnostic contract.
Inspect existing memory alarms; edit only if the current Terraform does not already satisfy the run-up alarm requirement.
